problem: Prior surveys on embodied AI simulators and navigation predate LLMs and world models, or treat simulator choice qualitatively or in simulation only. They rarely examine low-level simulator properties (contact solvers, actuation timing, sensor models, rendering) that determine sim-to-real outcomes across both navigation and manipulation.
motivation: Training embodied agents in the real world is costly, slow and unsafe, so simulation is central. But simulation success is often not predictive of hardware performance: agents exploit artifacts such as wall sliding, and contact solvers or timing models change manipulation outcomes. Researchers therefore need guidance on which simulator properties matter for which task, and on hardware constraints.
key_idea: Survey navigation and manipulation through the lens of physics-simulator properties, split into a perception gap and an action-dynamics gap, linking simulators, benchmarks, metrics and methods to sim-to-real predictivity and hardware needs.
insight: Small low-level simulator choices can flip sim-to-real outcomes, and success metrics like SR/SPL can hide unsafe or unrealistic behaviour. Evidence gathered in Table 1: tuned collision response raises SRCC on SPL from 0.603 to 0.875; V-REP Newton has much lower pose error than Bullet; modeling actuation noise and interpolation moves real assembly success from 0% to 50%. Simulator selection should therefore be task-driven (contact, vision, deformables, underwater, ROS deployment), not by generic feature checkmarks.
method: Sim-to-real framing: defines the gap G(π)=ψ_sim−ψ_real and SRCC, splits discrepancies into perception and action-dynamics gaps, and groups mitigations into calibration/explicit modeling, randomization, and transfer-oriented policy learning.

Navigation review: categorizes simulators (indoor, outdoor ground/air/underwater, general-purpose), goal-driven and task-driven benchmarks, metrics (SR, SPL, CLS, nDTW, ISR, EQA efficiency, IVR), and methods (explicit metric/graph memory; implicit latent, foundation-model, world-model).

Manipulation review: taxonomy of tasks (grasping, dexterous, deformable, fragile, mobile, open-world, bimanual), classical vs differentiable engines, decision table of simulators with failure modes, benchmarks, sensing modalities (vision, contact, visuo-tactile) and policy learning (RL, IL, ACT, diffusion, VLM, VLA).

Simulator comparison tables: compare physics engine, rendering, dynamics types, sensing, GPU and open-source support for manipulation and navigation platforms, with qualitative ratings of contact/soft/vision/deploy.

Discussion and error analysis: unification of navigation and manipulation (hierarchical vs shared latent-action/VLA), taxonomy of simulator-induced failures with checks/mitigations, and future directions (continual learning, neural ODEs, procedural and safety metrics).

setting.simulator: n/a (survey covers Habitat, AI2-THOR, Isaac Sim, MuJoCo, Genesis, CARLA, AirSim, HoloOcean, etc.)

numbers_note: Survey with no original experiments. Table 1 quotes other works' sim-to-real evidence, which is not this paper's own results.
results: As a survey, it reports no new experimental results. It compiles evidence that collision response, contact solver and actuation timing modeling strongly affect sim-to-real predictivity (SRCC 0.875 vs 0.603; real assembly success 50% vs 0%). It concludes that simulator selection should follow task-specific physical requirements and hardware constraints.
limitations: Qualitative ratings of simulators (High/Med/Low) are subjective and not benchmarked empirically.
Cited sim-to-real evidence is drawn from a few heterogeneous studies, and the survey has no unified quantitative comparison.
Navigation coverage of recent VLN/ObjectNav results is thin, with mostly dataset-level baseline SRs.
